checks.claim: Key: primary vs secondary succession is decided by whether soil is left (primary on barren substrate lacking soil; secondary after a disturbance that leaves the soil)

Wrong: whether returning plants match the old ones (not the definition)

Key: acids a lichen gives off weather the rock surface
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'By producing oxalic acid and other chelators, they break down silicate rocks.' Reviews (Adamo and Violante) name oxalic acid secreted by the mycobiont as among the most active weathering agents; hyphal penetration is a second, physical mechanism, but no choice claims it, so the key stands.

Piedmont NC old-field sequence: horseweed year 1, asters year 2, broomsedge from year 3, young pine forest years 19-30, hardwood transition 70-100, oak-hickory after 100
Scene: abandoned cotton field in the NC Piedmont

checks.claim: Key: hardwood seedlings grow in shade where young pines cannot
checks.note: Duke: pines cannot reproduce 'in their own shade'; shade-tolerant species grow beneath them. Duke also names greater soil-water use by the pines; 'shade does the work' is a fair 8th-grade simplification.

Wrong: hardwood root poison kills pines (no source supports it)

Henry Chandler Cowles studied the Lake Michigan (Indiana) dunes in the 1890s; published 1899 (Botanical Gazette)
checks.note: Grokipedia's Cowles page 404s; Grokipedia's Ecological succession page credits his 1899 Lake Michigan dune studies.

checks.claim: Sequence lake to inland: beach grass, cottonwoods, pines, oak forest
Key: bands are stages over time (space read as time); farthest dunes oldest
checks.note: UChicago: 'the linear succession of these communities in space also represented a linear progression in time.'

William S. Cooper set up plots at Glacier Bay in 1916 on recently deglaciated ground; revisited for a century (Cooper 25 years, Lawrence to late 1980s, relocated 2016)
checks.note: One plot had been bare about 24 years in 1916 (exposed ~1892); sources call the ground recently deglaciated or 'at a glacier's edge', so 'just left bare' is a fair simplification.

checks.claim: Willows invaded many plots in the 1920s and remain; alder and spruce rarer
Key: early arrivals can keep later ones out (inhibition / priority effect)
checks.note: Buma et al. 2017 (Ecology 98:1513): the plots 'do not support the classic facilitation model'; 'stochastic early community assembly and subsequent inhibition have dominated'; where Salix dominates there is no establishment of later species like Picea. NPS: pioneers 'monopolize resources and resist invasion'.

checks.claim: Wrong: willows are the final stage (spruce-hemlock forest grows on older ground at Bartlett Cove)
Wrong: ground loses species with age (species richness generally rose)
Wrong: ice-bared ground can never grow a forest
Context: dispersal limits far up the bay; richness rose over the century, most in the oldest plots near the bay's mouth
Mount St. Helens lateral blast out of the north flank, 18 May 1980
Pyroclastic flows near the crater laid down the Pumice Plain; blast flattened forest farther out
checks.note: Pyroclastic deposits 3-12 m on the pumice plain.

checks.claim: Key: blowdown zone kept survivors (late snow shielded plants; plants in soil on rootwads; resprouting from roots); none survived in the pyroclastic zone; survivors speed recovery
Wrong: open sunlight (the pumice plain was open too); leftover heat; thicker ash (pumice plain deposits were far thicker)
Context: prairie lupine was the first plant on the Pumice Plain two years after the eruption; dead stems trapped seeds and made a seedbed; leaves added nitrogen and organic matter

Gull colony from the mid-1980s (1984 per Wikipedia; 'after 1985' per Magnusson et al. 2014); 'some twenty years' holds

checks.note: Grokipedia: guano rich in marine-derived nitrogen and phosphorus; cover up to 90% in seabird areas vs ~7% elsewhere.

checks.note: Abstract: seabirds 'through their transfer of nutrients from sea to land, are major drivers'. 'The main force' is a close paraphrase.

checks.claim: Clements, Plant Succession (1916): one climax per climate, self-perpetuating; community likened to an organism that arises, grows, matures and dies
checks.note: Wikipedia quotes Clements 1916: 'As an organism the formation arises, grows, matures, and dies.'

checks.claim: Key: today a climax is seen as less fixed, since disturbance keeps resetting patches
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'the notion of a stable climax vegetation has been largely abandoned'; Grokipedia: climax now 'a transient or probabilistic configuration', patch dynamics.

checks.claim: Wrong: just as he said; random with no pattern; fixed but only in forests (Grokipedia lists grassland and chaparral climaxes)
Context: Gleason 1926 called a plant association 'merely a coincidence', not an organism
Context: Gleason challenged Clements 'as early as 1926'
checks.note: Gleason first challenged Clements in 1917 ('The Structure and Development of the Plant Association'); 1926 was the stronger, classic statement. 'As early as 1926' wrongly makes 1926 the start. Fix: 'Henry Gleason challenged Clements from 1917, and in 1926 called a plant community a coincidence rather than an organism.' (or simply 'in 1926').

checks.claim: Glacier-bared ground: crusts and mosses first, shrubs, forest by about two centuries (hemlock canopy ~200 years at Glacier Bay)

checks.note: MacArthur and MacArthur 1961 and later work across successional stages support it.

unit_notes: 9 ok, 1 error. The one error is in a context line (Gleason's challenge began 1917, not 1926). Glacier Bay key checked against Buma et al. 2017: 'stochastic early community assembly and subsequent inhibition have dominated', so the inhibition reading is the paper's own. Lichen weathering: oxalic acid from the fungal partner is the main chemical agent; hyphal penetration also acts physically, but no choice claims it. Grokipedia pages for Henry Chandler Cowles and Henry Gleason return 404; Wikipedia and UChicago were used instead.
